items.note: Study 2 randomizes 480 participants (160 each in English, Arabic, Chinese) to write business emails with or without AI-generated content; trained evaluators rate quality, actionability, and creativity. Study 1 rates AI-only output (context).

Participants write SAT-style essays over three sessions with an LLM, a search engine, or no tool, then 18 switch conditions in session 4; essays scored by teachers and an AI judge and analyzed for within-group homogeneity (n-grams, NER, topics), plus EEG; assignment method not stated in the abstract.

Two controlled experiments (562 participants total, split not stated; search notes suggest 247 in one) include a writing task with no LLM, one generalist assistant, or two role-specialized assistants; essay quality and idea diversity are measured on output; math experiment is out of scope.

32 university students write 64 creative essays with and without ChatGPT (paired within-person comparison); three expert writers rate assertions, opposing views, cases, concept quality, agency, and structure diversity; order randomization not stated; below 50 participants.

Semantic fluency (memory search) task; the abstract reports only that an LLM predicts human retrieval trajectories, but the title claims the LLM collaboratively modulates human search, so a human-with-AI condition may exist; full text needed, may turn out model-only.

Quasi-experiment with 84 Thai eleventh-graders in ChatGPT-integrated lessons versus conventional teaching; creative writing scored pre and post on a 5-point rubric (creativity, voice, literary devices); unclear whether AI was available at the post-test.

System paper (GraphStory, graph-based story ideation) with a user study of professional and semi-professional writers comparing it to normal AI-based writing workflows (ai_design); creativity support outcomes are likely self-reported; N not stated.
Design-course students use GenAI tools on projects and answer a questionnaire (N = 102) on perceived creativity factors; no comparison condition and no scored output.

Tool paper (GenFODrawing) with a 12-person user study comparing the GenAI tool with a baseline of participants' own methods on found-object drawing; outcomes (idea exploration, agency, creativity support) look self-reported; far below 50.

Quasi-experiment with two classes, one randomly assigned (class-level, not individual) to a ChatGPT-based flipped-learning guiding approach for a courseware project; outcomes are project performance and creative thinking (likely a self-report scale); N not stated; creativity task fit is doubtful.
